samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Orthniel Chambers, II was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Today is November 21, 2008, and we are at Good Samaritan Society, Las Cruces, New Mexico, where veteran Othniel Robert Chambers II is going to tell the story of his military experiences. Mr. Chambers was born in Austin, Texas, November 22, 1927. Tomorrow will be his 81st birthday. He now lives at 2975 Terrace Drive Apartment 310 in Las Cruces, New Mexico. He joined the United States Army as a young man. The interviewer is Louise Forshaw. Alright, Mr. Chambers, shall we begin?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: I started school two years ahead of everybody else, because the college in our town was doing research on 3 and 4 year-olds who could learn to read, so I was one of twenty-seven, I went through the public school system in Corvallis, Oregon, and I was two years younger than everybody else. So, when World War II came along, all of a sudden men, as they turned seventeen or eighteen, all the men disappeared. Even some of them came back as wounded veterans, but those who returned gave me a strange look and said, "Where the heck have you been? You a chicken or something?" So, my dad would not let me lie about my age, and would not let me join at seventeen. On my eighteenth birthday I went downtown and enlisted, because I owed it to all of my fellow students, had to enlist three times in two days, actually, because I had a bad arm. The third time they said, "Well, if you want in that bad." Reported to Fort Lewis up in Washington, I enlisted in Corvallis, Oregon at Fort Lewis, they dressed me like a soldier and sent me to Camp Roberts in California, where I spent - at that time basic training was eight weeks. Despite the fact I missed a week of that training because I had pneumonia, I was immediately sent back to Fort Lewis where I was held as a replacement for...I don't know if it was National Guard or Reserve...for the 107th Ordnance out of Pontiac, Michigan. They were short eight people for a full table of organization, so I was sent in as a company clerk, because I had had some college education, and they wanted somebody who could read and write.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: What does a company clerk do?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: Well, have you ever watched M.A.S.H.?

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: [Laughter] Well, company clerk keeps the records for the company and the individuals. He backs up the first sergeant in passing out orders, making sure they get around, does what is asked of him in the way of duties around the camp as requested by the commander. Ours was a mobile unit, we tried to stay fairly close to the artillery up near the front but not at the front, and we had a TO of two hundred and nine men I think it was. But we had something like two hundred and twenty pieces of mobile equipment. Jeeps, trucks, tanks, all sorts of things. And we said, "If it's not working, bring it in and we'll fix it." Even to the point where we occasionally fixed a helicopter. A few of our people, a few times went out at night with armloads of weapons and crawled from foxhole to foxhole saying, "Is there anything wrong with your weapons, do you want to trade?"

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Now, this was when?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: This was in Korea, in the spring of - oh wait a minute, I'm way ahead of myself.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: That's okay. Let's go back to when you were at Fort Lewis and you were made company clerk.

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: That was in Korea. The second time.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Well, let's finish your second time and we can go back to that.

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: Our people, the ones from Pontiac, Michigan, had just taken a good look and decided that the only way they were ever going to go home was to go make sure that the war was won as quickly as possible. So, they passed two unspoken rules, one was "You tell us where it's broken, and we'll trade you there." And the other was, "If you have a piece of equipment with somebody in it who's alive, and they can't be moved, tell us where it is and we'll go get it, if we can." And one result, we had a truck, well actually we had two trucks that were designed to carry tanks. And on one occasion one of those trucks went out, [inaudible] found the tank, pulled the tank up onto the truck, started south, and passed some Marines going north who got blasted right where our truck had been because the Chinese and North Koreans had been sitting up on the hill above it, and they figured we'd send somebody else. The thing that struck me, as I think about the most, was our company was associated for quite a while with the Korean Infantry Company. I made friends with a couple of people there. When we moved, their idea of a good meal was build a bonfire and put a fifty gallon drum in the middle of it. Fill it half full of water with rice and start adding anything you can find. But the first day it was wonderful, with rabbit and all kinds of things in it, and then you get down to vegetables, and then it was just plain rice, the area was denuded. So they were very glad to be close to us to get additional supplies from us. A fellow that I knew was named Cha Chung Tae.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Do you know how to spell that?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: C-H-A C-H-U-N-G, T-A-E. And at one point we were close to, within twenty or thirty miles of his hometown. So I talked the C.O. into letting him have a three day leave. Because he hadn't seen his family since the war started. When he came back, he brought me back a bowl, chopsticks, a serving spoon, and a small bowl with a lid and his name and mine were engraved in the top. His father was a copper worker. Very good. But he couldn't get any copper so he ruined his tools making this set out of artillery brass. I still have them, by the way, with his name and mine. Tae and Chambers. But, people were that desperate. He felt a need, just the fact that he could see his son, alive, that he would ruin a bunch of copper work tools to make a gift in exchange. Another thing that struck me, when we went north, civilians were streaming down the road on foot. Women's dress for the lower classes was a pair of trousers that came up to just underneath the breast and down to cuffed ankles and then a little bolero jacket. In the summertime the difference was they took off the T-shirt. And there they went, they took it off from underneath the jacket. One day I was sitting beside the road, it dawned on me, I said, "Gee it's been months since I've seen an ankle." But people didn't care about nudity up above because, that was their custom.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Now, you're telling us about your experiences in Korea. How did you get to Korea? How did you travel to the states?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: We took a ship. Traveled by ship, they had about five thousand people aboard. We went directly from Seattle to a port roughly twenty miles south of Tokyo. It was a former Japanese Naval base. As I said, every morning we'd fall out ready to go, and be told we had to wait another day.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Tell us a little about that, your base in Japan. What kind of base was it?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: I believe it was a Navy Officer's training base.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: And what were your living conditions?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: We lived in dormitories, a couple of them, anyway. Beds spread out around the edge of each room. The restrooms were interesting, to me, because instead of having urinals, they simply tiled one wall and put a drop in the bottom. The wash basin was a single big circle with spray coming down all around it.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Now, you mention that each day you got ready -

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: We were expecting to be transshipped to Korea. But apparently, there was literally no place that a ship could dock. So every morning we got up early enough that we were standing out at attention fully, with all of our gear on at six a.m. and then they'd say, "Sorry about that, you're free to go."

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Then you'd be dismissed.

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: I was really very amazed, of course, by that time Japan was used to having us around. So I never encountered anyone who seemed antagonistic toward me. Matter of fact, one day I was out wandering around and some farm people, were working on building a house. I stood out on the road there, and they were down in the field. I was watching, and they were weaving - first they drove in wood stakes, then they wove small branches through it and made a pattern, then they dropped straw into mud and brought it over like adobe, and patted it in. I got so interested I forgot what I was doing, and ended up very closely watching. Finally, they said, "Would you like to help?" I said, "Yeah." So I helped to make a wall, and then lunchtime came and they brought out some soup, we all had soup together and I had a wonderful afternoon. They couldn't speak any English, I couldn't speak any Japanese, but I saw how they built the house.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: At some point you did get over to Korea, didn't you?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: Oh yes. It was the 31st or 32nd day. Just enough to get the Japanese Occupation title.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: And what were your duties in Korea? To back up the artillery?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: No, we were a maintenance ordinance. So we were in the business of fixing things. We tried to stay up close simply because the closer we were the quicker things got fixed.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: What was it like? What was Korea like in terms of living conditions?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: For me, you mean?

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: For you and your friends in the military.

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: Well, we lived in tents and we ate quite well, supplies were usually pretty good. We usually had a pretty heavy perimeter guard around our camp. But people left the camp regularly. If they heard anything needed repair, they'd go get it. So, there was one time when I was absolutely fascinated, an outfit was being driven south, and somebody blew the bridge over a ravine ahead of them. So they deliberately ran one hundred vehicles off over the cliff, rather than leave them behind for the Chinese. Everybody went north again. We were set up right close there. The Engineer Corps looked at it, the 8th Army looked at it, and finally Far Eastern Command looked at it and everybody said, "Hey forgot it, it's not worth it." But we wanted parts, so one of our sergeants made a deal and periodically they would close the pass and we had a couple of heavy tanks clear up above and bulldozers, and pushed rocks together, ran a cable down, and then anytime they'd close the road we'd throw the cable down and we'd already have someone down at the bottom hook the cable onto something and drag it up. I think they actually pulled back up all but one piece. We used the parts.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Ingenuity, isn't it?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: Yes. And the sergeant that made the deal, told the company commander to give him punishment for not paying attention to orders, and they did. His punishment was relief of all duty, sent to Japan with a five day pass, and every fifth day they'd send him another pass. He haunted the docks, and every time he saw something going to a company that he knew for sure was not any place close to the enemy, he used a spray can and changed the address and the parts came to us. So we were pretty well fixed up.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: You and your men were pretty eager to do a good job?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: The outfit was all but nine people from Pontiac, Michigan, a reserve unit or something, and they were all interrelated you know. The company commanders brother was married to the - and so on. They very, very quickly came to the conclusion that, "If we don't do our flat level best, we ain't gonna get to go home. So the quicker we do this the quicker we go home."

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: When did you complete your service in Korea?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: Right on time. I was due for discharge, and so they sent me home in October. Let's see, I started in September of '51 and didn't get there ‘til October. I had already made plans. I looked at a map and figured out where the four year University furthest from Korea was. I stopped in Corvallis for two days, then caught a plane for Miami, Florida, and went to the University of Miami on the G.I. Bill.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Okay. Now Mr. Chambers, can we go back to your first active duty, that was when you enlisted at eighteen in 1945?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: I reported to Fort Ord, was promptly sent to Camp Roberts in California, which was at that time the camp reputed to have the largest parade ground in the United States. I don't know whether that was just talk or real, but it seemed like anytime we went any place or did anything it was on the other side of the parade ground. We got our eight weeks of training, I had a week of pneumonia. We were immediately, almost immediately, were sent on to New Jersey. We were only there for about three days, then put on a ship and went to La Havre. As I said, on those ships they crammed about four or five thousand people on them. It was wintertime when we went through the north Atlantic.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Did you get up on deck very much?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: I didn't get off deck. Somewhere I still have the meal card they punch every time. The first three meals are punched, then there's one out in the middle that's punched, and there's two or three clear at the other end, and the rest of the time I was lying on the deck. Because everytime I went down the combination of heat and body odor, I couldn't handle it, with the ship's movement.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Where did you go after La Havre?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: We were sent to a camp in France, not too far from La Havre. Then in a matter of a day or two they loaded us on cattle cars and we were all sent to the units who wanted us. I was sent to Bamberg, Germany and took a different train, and went down to - we ended up in Vienna, we went right by Dachau on the way. What's the name of the town where Oktoberfest is?

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Munich?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: Munich. Yeah, we went to Munich and we went on over to Vienna.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Were you right in Vienna or were you - ?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: Yes, as a matter of fact, headquarters had taken over - the Americans had taken over the buildings and the complex of the National Bank. So the A.G.'s office was the National Bank building. I was housed seven or eight blocks up the street in an apartment complex. Walked back and forth. For the dining room they took over one of the best restaurants in town.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: And you were company clerk? Or what were your duties?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: No, I don't really know what I was - I was a corporal [Laughter].

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: What did they have you do?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: I was sorting records and organizing them, primarily. Handling other paperwork as required. Officially eight to five, but essentially "Here's what you have to do today and then you can go." Which usually turned out to be more like eight or nine. It was very difficult for me to eat in the dining room. Because it had a big plate glass window in the front which you'd enter. And food at that time was desperately scarce. So they had an MP shaking you down when you left, make sure you didn't smuggle any out to give to anybody. So you'd sit there eating, and noses were pressed to the glass frequently. Mostly little kids. By that time - well, Vienna was at that time not antagonistic toward us, it was toward the Russians mostly.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Can you describe for your listeners what the situation was with the four zones?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: The center inside the inner ring was an international zone, and then the far zones were just like cutting out pieces of pie. One of my favorite places to visit was Schoenbrun Castle, which is way out to the west.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Can I ask you to spell that?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: S-C-H-O-E-N-B-R-U-N. So it's Schoenburn Palace, actually. That was the British Army headquarters. I spent quite a bit of time their because it was a very beautiful place.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: There was a Russian zone -

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: A French zone, an American and an English. Schoenburn was English headquarters. I never did quite figure out exactly where France's section was. But everything on the other side of the river, the other side of the Danube was Russia. The airport was at a place called "Tuln," T-U-L-N. So you had to drive through the Russian zone in order to get there and come back. One of my duties was to go to Tuln and meet the plane, deliver people who were coming back. The Russians got the point, "Hi Joe." If you were not somebody that the guards knew, you were checked.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: I think you told me earlier, that at night boats would go into the river?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: First thing in the morning.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Would you describe that for our listeners?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: There were two motor launches down at the rivers edge, and each launch had a German policeman and a soldier, usually a sergeant from each of the other four countries, and their job was to go down river for a while and then turned around, came back up and went up river so they got a good section, and they'd pick up any bodies that might be floating and brought them onto the dock. Some days they didn't find anybody, some days they found several.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: When did you leave your duties in Vienna?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: Would have been in August or September of 1947.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: And how did you get back to the States?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: I don't remember exactly. I think it was by train to France, then troop ship to the U.S.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Alright, were you discharged when you returned to the States?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: We went back, I think it was by train, to La Havre, and then from La Havre to New York. In New York they gave me a forty eight hour pass and then went back to camp, and they handed me a discharge. They provided me with discharge money, enough to get me home. But I made my own way, went by bus.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: You were a civilian from 1947 until you were called back to active duty in 1950.

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: How did you spend those years?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: I spent about a year at Oregon State University, failed miserably because I couldn't pay attention. Went to work for the railroad for a while, came back to Corvallis, and worked in a women's clothing store for a Frenchman who did just about all the fitting himself. Then one night the place burned. Burned clear to the ground, and I was the last person there so I spent the rest of my time going where I wanted, but I had to report my current address to the state fire marshal. Fortunately, I had worked my way through high school with the U.S. Forest Service, first as a fire crewman then as a lookout, and so I came back then, when the place burned I had just at that point made contact and been offered a job as a survey crewman for the U.S. Forest Service in northern Arizona. Just on the edge there, so that was the job I was in when I got the letter.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: When you were recalled to active duty, alright now let's skip ahead to when you were discharged from active service in Korea. What work did you do in the years following that period?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: By that time I had gotten mad. "They can't do this to me." I had been thrown out of too many schools. So I buckled down, started making straight A's. Oregon State University, OSU, in Corvallis, was kind enough to let me back in until I could legitimately get a transfer. So I got several straight A's and drove a taxi during that time. That was fun. Six days a week from six in the morning until six in the evening. Then classes four nights a week from seven to ten. Which was interesting.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Ultimately, what was your work career?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: I went to University of Oregon, of course. I met a gal there and married her. Graduated and spent one year in Graduate school. She was pregnant and the baby was born right at the end of finals week. My advisor, this after one year of Grad school, my advisor knew somebody in the state of Washington, and he sent me up there. I was accepted and went to work as a guard in the Washington State Reformatory.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: So you were in corrections work?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: I stayed in corrections work. Three years later I had been promoted to a parole officer. I followed the warden down to a new institution in Salem, Oregon where I helped design and organize staff and training. I worked there for thirteen years, working up from sociologist to acting assistant superintendent. Then they wanted to get rid of me, but couldn't catch me doing anything wrong. So they promoted me over to be Executive Assistant to the State Administrator of Corrections. I spent another sixteen years there.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: So, all in all how many years did you spend in corrections"?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: Thirty-two.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: You mentioned being married. How many children did you have?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: Four.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: And when did you move to New Mexico?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: When I retired in early 1988, my wife all of a sudden pulled out this whole drawer full of materials she had gotten from real estate people in the south. Because she spent the first eight years of her life in Mexico, so we sold the house, bought a fifth wheel and a truck, and for just under three years we travelled back and forth between California and Florida looking for someplace that we could agree to live in. Then in the fall of 1990 we stopped here. She liked it and I was willing to live here, so we moved to Las Cruces.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Now, Mr. Chambers, as you look back over the time you spent in the military, do you have any thoughts about benefits or disadvantages of military service?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: I learned to take orders, whether I liked them or not. I learned to keep my attitudes and my opinions to myself. I learned that you don't stop a job until a job is done, whatever that means. I also learned that people I met all over the world, almost everybody, was willing to be friendly if you gave them the opportunity.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Do you belong to any military organizations?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: No. I really don't consider myself a veteran. Because all of the things that so many people have had to go through, the injuries they've taken, the psychiatric difficulties, I didn't have any of that.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: As you know, your story is being preserved for future generations. Is there anything you'd like to say either about military experience or about life in general to the people who will be coming after this?

sp.speaker: Orthniel Chambers, II
sp.p: The military is necessary only when everything else fails. And even then, only when your existence, really, is threatened by the situation. Everybody deserves to be listened to. Usually, if you listen you'll discover you have a lot in common and you can build on that.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: We thank you very much, Niel Chambers, this completes our interview with Niel Chambers.
